summary: Discusses deployment issues and requirements for operating Dual-Stack Lite, covering the deployment considerations and applicability of the DS-Lite architecture. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A guide for running a system that lets old-style addresses be carried over new-style networks, with tips on what to plan for.

subtitle: Operating a system that runs IPv4 over IPv6 networks

tldr.problem: Internet service providers need to offer IPv4 services while upgrading their networks to IPv6, since IPv4 addresses are exhausted. They need guidance on deploying and operating DS-Lite, a technique that tunnels IPv4 packets over IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: DS-Lite tunnels IPv4 packets inside IPv6 packets between customer devices (B4) and a central router (AFTR) that performs network address translation. The AFTR translates packets between the IPv6 network and the IPv4 internet, allowing many customers to share public IPv4 addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6908 is informational and provides operational experience from real deployments. It does not define the DS-Lite protocol itself but rather describes best practices and considerations for deploying it.

today: RFC 6908 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted. It provides guidance for operators who deploy DS-Lite, a technique still used in some regions during the transition to IPv6.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: DS-Lite combines two techniques: IPv4-in-IPv6 tunneling and Network Address Translation (NAT) to let Internet service providers continue offering IPv4 services while operating mostly-IPv6 networks. The RFC explains real deployment challenges and solutions based on operator experience, instead of requiring operators to hunt through multiple RFCs.
sections.eli5: When Internet providers switch networks from old-style to new-style addresses, they need a way to keep old-style services working. This RFC collects lessons learned about how to do that.

sections.title: The AFTR and its Deployment
sections.content:
The Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) is the centerpiece of DS-Lite. It sits at the IPv4-IPv6 network border, terminating tunnels from customer devices and performing NAT. The RFC covers practical choices: whether to use one or two physical interfaces, how to handle IP fragmentation when the tunnel overhead reduces available packet size, and where to place AFTRs for best performance.

The document recommends sizing the AFTR based on deployment location: small AFTRs at the network edge serve fewer customers but reduce infrastructure costs, while larger AFTRs at the core serve more customers but require more powerful hardware.
sections.eli5: The AFTR is the special box that sits between the old-style and new-style networks. It needs to be sized right: small and local, or big and central?

sections.title: Operations and Logging
sections.content:
Operating an AFTR introduces challenges not present in normal IPv4 NAT. The AFTR must log which IPv6 customer address maps to which temporary IPv4 address, with source port ranges, to help track down problem users. The RFC describes source-specific logging (recording incoming port and address) versus destination-specific logging (also recording what the customer talks to), noting that destination-specific logging creates far more log entries.

When multiple customers share one IPv4 address, blacklisting that address (for spam, for example) affects all users behind it. The RFC notes this asymmetry and suggests geographically-aware services may give incorrect location information since all traffic appears to come from the AFTR's location, not the customer's actual location.
sections.eli5: Shared addresses cause problems: if one person misbehaves, everyone behind the shared address gets blocked. Logs must track who did what, which can be a lot of data. Services that guess where you are from your address will guess wrong.

sections.title: Reliability and Service Control
sections.content: The RFC recommends operators deploy multiple AFTRs for reliability, with Cold Standby mode (sessions are lost on failover, but simpler to operate) preferred over Hot Standby mode (sessions survive failover, but more complex). DS-Lite policies control which IPv6 customers can access the AFTR, and QoS policies can prioritize traffic. Port forwarding (letting an incoming connection reach a customer behind NAT) requires either UPnP, the Port Control Protocol, or manual configuration.
sections.eli5: Having backup AFTRs means if one fails, service can continue. The AFTR can decide which customers get priority, whether to let specific ports through, and block troublemakers.

sections.title: Integration with Network Services
sections.content: DS-Lite affects accounting (traffic measurement), since IPv4 traffic is hidden inside IPv6 packets. Operators can measure at the edge router (seeing the IPv6 container) or at the AFTR (seeing the IPv4 content), each with trade-offs. DNS service requires careful attention: the RFC recommends customers use IPv6 DNS, with the B4 proxy translating IPv4 DNS queries if needed, following RFC 5625 guidelines. B4 devices should be monitored and managed over native IPv6, not tunneled through the softwire.
sections.eli5: Counting traffic is tricky when the real traffic is hidden inside the tunnel. DNS lookups need special handling. The AFTR needs a way to stay reachable for management.
